What Green Laning Actually Is

Green laning UK style is the simple, deeply rewarding practice of riding a road-legal motorcycle along unsurfaced public rights of way: the ancient tracks, drove roads and byways that criss-cross the British countryside. It is not off-roading in the sense of blasting across open moorland or private fields, and it is not enduro racing. It is quiet, legal exploration of lanes that have carried carts, livestock and travellers for centuries and remain, in the eyes of the law, public highways. Done properly it opens up a Britain most road riders never see, and it can be enjoyed on everything from a lightweight trail bike to a fully loaded adventure machine like the KTM 890 Adventure.

I have spent years riding lanes across Wales, the Peak District and the South West, and the single most important thing I can teach a beginner is this: the whole activity depends on you riding only where you are legally entitled to, and doing so in a way that keeps those lanes open for everyone. Get that right and green laning is one of the most satisfying things you can do on two wheels. Get it wrong and you damage the countryside, anger other users, and hand ammunition to those who would close the network entirely.

The Law: Which Lanes Can You Ride?

This is where every beginner must start, and where most confusion lies. In England and Wales, a right of way that you can legally ride a motor vehicle on falls, broadly, into two categories. The clearest is the Byway Open to All Traffic, or BOAT. These are shown on Ordnance Survey maps and are lawful for motorcycles, cars, horses, cyclists and walkers alike. If a lane is a recorded BOAT, you are entitled to ride it.

The second category is the Unclassified County Road, or UCR, sometimes called an unclassified road or unsurfaced unclassified road. These are genuine public roads that simply have never been surfaced. They carry full vehicular rights but they are recorded on the local highway authority's List of Streets rather than always appearing clearly as byways on a map, which makes them harder to identify with certainty.

You will also come across RUPPs, or Roads Used as Public Paths. This was an old classification that has largely been reclassified, most often into restricted byways, under the Countryside and Rights of Way Act. A Restricted Byway allows walkers, horses, cyclists and horse-drawn carriages but crucially does not permit mechanically propelled vehicles, so you cannot ride a motorcycle on one. Bridleways and footpaths are likewise off limits to motorcycles. Finally, be aware of the Traffic Regulation Order, or TRO, a legal tool a council can use to close or restrict a lane, seasonally or permanently, for reasons such as preventing damage. A lane that was legal last year may carry a TRO this year.

The golden rule for a beginner: never assume a lane is legal because a tyre track runs down it. Confirm its status before you ride, every single time, and if you cannot confirm it, do not ride it.

Rights of Way and How to Check Them

The Definitive Map, held by each local authority, is the legal record of public rights of way, but it does not always show UCRs. The practical tools most laners rely on are the resources maintained by the Green Lane Association, known as GLASS, whose Trailwise database maps researched, ridable lanes and their current status. An OS map with the 1:25,000 detail helps you read the ground, but map colours alone are not proof of vehicular rights. When in doubt, contact the local highway authority's rights of way officer. It is slow, unglamorous work, but it is the foundation of legal laning.

GLASS and the Rider's Code

The Green Lane Association is the national body representing recreational motorised users of green lanes, and joining is one of the best things a beginner can do. Membership gives you access to Trailwise, a community of experienced laners, and a body that fights legal battles to keep lanes open. GLASS also promotes a responsible riding code that every rider should treat as gospel.

  • Ride only lanes with confirmed public vehicular rights, and respect all TROs and seasonal closures.
  • Keep to established routes and never widen a lane or create new lines around obstacles or puddles.
  • Travel at a considerate speed, especially near homes, livestock, walkers and horses.
  • Ride in small groups, ideally no more than four or five bikes, to limit noise and wear.
  • Leave gates as you find them, and take all litter home.
  • Never ride when a lane is so wet that you will cause lasting damage. If you are churning it up, turn back.

Choosing a Bike for Green Laning

You do not need the biggest, most expensive machine. In fact, for a beginner, lighter is almost always better. A heavy adventure bike is a handful when the going gets soft or steep, and picking it up when you drop it, which you will, is exhausting. A lightweight trail bike or a small-capacity adventure bike is far more forgiving while you learn.

Excellent starting points include the Royal Enfield Himalayan 450, which is genuinely manageable off road, and the Honda CB500X for those who want a do-it-all bike that dabbles in the lanes. If you are set on something with more adventure credentials, the Yamaha Tenere 700 is a firm favourite among laners for its balance of capability and relative simplicity. For a deeper look at the options, read our guide to mid-weight adventure bikes and our overview of how to tour on an adventure bike, since many laning trips fold naturally into wider touring.

Basic Technique for the Lanes

Green laning technique is mostly about smoothness and vision rather than heroics. Stand on the pegs when the surface turns loose or rough. Standing lowers your effective centre of gravity through the footpegs, frees the bike to move beneath you, and lets your legs soak up the bumps. Grip the tank with your knees, keep your elbows up, and look well ahead to where you want to go rather than at the obstacle right in front of the wheel.

Use gentle, progressive throttle to keep the rear driving without spinning up, and let the engine do the braking on descents by staying in a low gear. On my early rides I made every classic mistake: too fast, too stiff, staring at the front wheel and grabbing the front brake on loose gravel. Slow down, breathe, and treat the throttle and brakes like they are made of glass. Tyres matter too, and our adventure tyre guide explains the trade-offs between road-biased and knobbly rubber that make a real difference in the dirt.

Staying Legal and Being Considerate

Your bike must be fully road legal for every lane you ride: taxed, insured, MOT'd where applicable, with a number plate, working lights and legal tyres. Green lanes are public roads, so all the normal road rules apply. There is no such thing as riding a green lane on an unregistered pit bike; that is illegal off-roading and it is exactly what gets lanes closed.

Consideration is the other half of the coin. Green lanes are shared with walkers, horse riders, cyclists and, near villages, residents whose homes back onto them. Slow right down and give way generously. Cut your engine or idle past horses, which can be badly spooked by revving. A friendly wave and a low speed do more to protect the future of green laning than any amount of legal argument. Ride as if a landowner or a rambler is watching, because often one is.

Where to Go Next

Once you understand the law and have a suitable bike, the countryside opens up. Start with well-documented lanes in your area, ideally with an experienced rider or a GLASS group, and build confidence gradually. From there, explore our guide to the best green lanes in the UK, sort out your kit with our green laning gear essentials, and when you are ready for a bigger challenge, look at the Trans Euro Trail UK section. Ride legal, ride light, and leave every lane exactly as you found it.
keyTakeaways: Green laning means riding a road-legal bike on unsurfaced public rights of way, not open moorland.
You may ride Byways Open to All Traffic (BOATs) and Unclassified County Roads, but not bridleways or restricted byways.
Always confirm a lane's legal status before riding, as a tyre track is no proof of vehicular rights.
Lighter bikes are far more forgiving for beginners than heavy adventure machines.
The GLASS Trailwise database is the key tool for checking researched, ridable lanes.

faq.q: Which lanes can I legally ride a motorcycle on?
faq.a: In England and Wales you may ride Byways Open to All Traffic, which are shown on OS maps and lawful for all traffic, and Unclassified County Roads, which are genuine public roads recorded on the highway authority's List of Streets. You cannot ride restricted byways, bridleways or footpaths, and you must respect any Traffic Regulation Order. Never assume a lane is legal because a tyre track runs down it.

faq.q: How do I check a lane's legal status?
faq.a: The Definitive Map held by each local authority is the legal record, but it does not always show Unclassified County Roads. Most laners rely on the Green Lane Association's Trailwise database, which maps researched, ridable lanes and their current status. Cross-check with a 1:25,000 OS map, but remember map colours alone are not proof of vehicular rights. When in doubt, contact the local rights of way officer, or do not ride.

A heavy adventure bike is a handful when the going gets soft or steep, and exhausting to pick up when you drop it, which you will. Manageable starting points include the Royal Enfield Himalayan 450, the Honda CB500X for a do-it-all bike, and the Yamaha Tenere 700 for more adventure credentials.

Ride considerately, give way generously, and leave gates as you find them.
